title: Grey Columns
eyebrow: Fixed and on your board: why every heading but Agent Review went grey

actions.fyi: You caught it exactly right, and it is back. One colour in eighteen was reaching your board; all eighteen do now, counted off a real build rather than argued about. A check goes red the moment one goes missing again.

content.label: What you saw, and why
content.lead: The colours were never wrong. They were never built.

rows.title: The colours moved house
rows.note: The recent columns work pulled every state's colour out of the screen parts and into one place, so that adding a state adds its colour everywhere at once. That was the right move and it is why the six columns could be added at all.

rows.title: The tool that builds the screen was never told about the new place
rows.note: It only ever writes out colours it has literally seen spelled somewhere, and it is given a short list of places to look. That list names three; the new home for the colours is not one of them. So it read the new file never, found the colours nowhere, and wrote none of them.

rows.title: Agent Review survived by accident
rows.note: Its colour happens to also be spelled by hand in the sessions panel and the activity list, which are in places the tool does look at. That one spelling is the entire set of colours your board still has.

rows.title: Everything reading from the one place went grey
rows.note: That is the six column headings, their count badges, their top rules, and the status dot beside every piece listed under a card. The screen asked for a colour, got nothing back, and drew the plain text colour instead.

blocks.text: Taken as: put the missing colours back and hold them there. Not to change which colour a state has — those are right where they are written — and not to restyle anything else on the board while in there.

content.label: Counted, not guessed
content.lead: The six states ask for eighteen colour rules between them — a colour to write in, a top rule for the column, a count badge. Here is how many your board actually had, and has now.

blocks.text: One of eighteen before, eighteen of eighteen after. The after is counted off the stylesheet the app is serving you now, fetched from the running board rather than read out of the source. The survivor was the accident described above, not something the board meant to keep.

content.label: What went in
content.lead: One line, and a check so it cannot happen quietly again.

rows.title: The fix
rows.note: The list of places the screen builder looks at went from three named ones to the whole of the screen source. Nothing about the colours themselves changed; they were already correct where they live. Both pieces are merged and on your board now.

rows.title: The check
rows.note: A new one builds the screen for real and demands that every colour each of the six states asks for came out the other side. It reads the states off the same one list the board does, so a seventh state brings its own colours into the check with it and nobody has to remember. It carries its own proof of teeth: a case that puts the fault back and insists colours go missing. A third case covers the dot beside a piece by the exact name the card list calls, so your second symptom is held separately from the columns. All 108 of the screen's own test files come back green with it in.

rows.title: What it does not fix
rows.note: Colours spelled by hand in four screen parts stay spelled by hand. They are not wrong today, but they are the same trap a second time — they are what hid this one — and there is a card on the board for pulling them into the one place too.

rows.title: Why your screen still looked broken after the fix landed
rows.note: The board you open is served by an installed copy of the app, built before any of this. Fixing the source does not touch it — it had to be rebuilt and put back in place. That is done: the copy you run was replaced and restarted, and the count below is taken from what it is serving you right now, not from the source.

rows.title: Something else came up while counting
rows.note: The screen's test run and its type check both swept the separate working copies kept inside the project, so they went red on files nobody is working on — 78 test files failing, every one inside a copy, none in the project itself. It predates this job, but it also stopped the app being rebuilt at all, so it had to be fixed here: 108 files green, no type errors, and the rebuild can run.

decisions.title: Widen where the screen builder looks, rather than copying the colours back into a place it already reads
decisions.why: Copying them back would undo the change that made six columns possible, and the same trap would spring for the next thing moved out of a screen part. The list of places to look was simply never updated when the colours moved.

decisions.title: The whole of the screen source, not just the one place the colours now live
decisions.why: Naming that one place would leave the identical hole open for the next file. The cost of looking at everything is a fraction of a second at build time, once.

decisions.title: The check builds the screen for real instead of reading the source and reasoning about it
decisions.why: Reasoning about it is exactly what missed this. The only honest question is whether the colour came out the far end, so that is what is asked.

next.if_nothing: Your board draws its six columns and every status dot in colour again and keeps them, and a check goes red if one ever goes missing. Nothing here is waiting on you.

steps.step: Reload your board — each column heading and each status dot is in its own colour again
Pull the last four hand-spelled colours into the one place, so the trap cannot spring twice
